extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, and researchers of news production
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and analyze the routines, constraints, and institutional standards that shape news selection, production, and presentation in print and broadcast media. Focuses on how organizational, occupational, and technological routines produce recurring distortions and selection patterns in news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story as narrative/drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Every news story should, without any sacrifice of probability or responsibility, display the attributes of fiction, of drama. It should have structure and conflict, problem and denouement, rising action and falling action, a beginning, a middle and an end. (Reuven Frank memo quoted)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion guides reporters in deciding which facts to include when transforming events into a news commodity; adopting a dramatic narrative helps make stories compelling but may shape which facts are selected or emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic thrust and villain construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are often treated like melodramas that identify heroes, victims, and clear villains (example: Iranian hostage crisis portrayed with hostages as heroes and Iranian militants as villains).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dramatic thrust that requires a clear villain can prevent reporters from giving a more comprehensive picture of complex conflicts and can impose an anti- or pro- orientation (e.g., anti-Iranian, anti-Islamic, pro-U.S. government). Visual symbols and melodramatic language heighten this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story format constraints (plot-fit distortion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story format constrains the reporter to organize facts to fit the plot line; transforming events into a beginning-middle-end can distort reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational pressure to construct a compelling plot (e.g., for prime-time competition) can lead producers to violate news guidelines (e.g., failing to pursue contrary information), as in the CBS 'A Vietnam Deception' case where the need for a clear plot led to distortion and breaches of internal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values are necessary but not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: News must have news value to be included, but news value alone is not sufficient to explain selection — some high-value stories go underreported (Project Censored examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because news values are often derived post hoc from existing content, they rationalize selections already made. Analysts should therefore look beyond audience appeal to organizational and occupational routines to explain exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-oriented routines have limited influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience figures least prominently in many news routines; journalists often write primarily for themselves, editors, and other journalists and are suspicious of audience research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists' reluctance to accept audience research and tendency to value professional autonomy means audience preference often does not strongly shape news selection or presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gatekeeper and source-proportion constraints (wire service influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual gatekeepers exercise subjective choice but are constrained by source formats such as the wire service menu; editors tend to select stories in proportions similar to their sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments and re-analyses show editors follow the proportions contained in their source copy; when sources vary, editors follow them, and when sources present equal categories, editors rely more on subjective judgment. Thus source-provided menus structure organizational agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational routines to manage physical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Routines (e.g., bureaus, beats, fixed news holes, deadlines) are developed to help organizations cope with limited space, time, and staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beats and bureaus ensure a steady, predictable stream of news and reduce the organization's reporting responsibility; deadlines produce temporal gaps (events outside newsday have less chance of coverage) and encourage coverage that fits schedules and available resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadlines and timing shape newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations 'live by the clock'; events must mesh with the organization's temporal spokes and cogs to be reported (Michael Schudson quote).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists seek coincident and convenient news near deadlines; politicians and sources schedule events with deadlines in mind (to gain or minimize coverage). This emphasis on timeliness disadvantages slowly developing stories and hinders advocacy journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard news vs soft news determined by scheduling
rubrics_metrics.description: The hard news/soft news distinction is less about content and more about how events are scheduled: hard news comes from prescheduled or unscheduled events that must be reported quickly; soft news (features) is nonscheduled and can be run when convenient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This scheduling perspective ('news net') leads organizations to typify events as newsworthy based on how they fit organizational timetables rather than intrinsic importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beats and news net create investment-driven selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters deployed to beats and bureaus produce a 'news net' of expected events; organizations use stories from those beats partly because they have invested resources (e.g., reporter salary) in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when editors and reporters agree nothing is happening on a beat, reporters are often obliged to produce something; this institutional investment biases selection toward beat-related happenings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predefined angles and script-driven reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters commonly approach stories with a predefined 'angle' or anticipated 'script' about how a story will unfold, leading them to seek supportive sources and details (Altheide study and freeway reporter transcript).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipated scripts lead reporters to favor familiar or predictable sources whose responses can be anticipated; more reporting time may yield more detail but not necessarily a more complete or less biased story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event routine preference (event pegs and visual necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media prefer events because they are unambiguous, defensible as news, and provide visual material (television); issue stories often require an event 'peg' to be covered widely (examples: Jessica McClure baby rescue; Tonya Harding/Nancy Kerrigan scandal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events provide focus and scheduling anchors; the visual nature of television especially demands 'something to record,' which favors event-centered coverage over long-term issue coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermedia influence and pack mentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists rely heavily on other media and each other for story ideas and confirmation, producing pack coverage and consistency across outlets (e.g., networks opening with identical Reagan video clip).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In an ambiguous environment journalists use consensus and consistency with peers as a risk-reduction strategy; this 'pack' behavior reinforces similar agendas across organizations and can marginalize dissenting or novel reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on authoritative outlets to certify stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain media (e.g., New York Times for international, Washington Post for national issues) serve as certifiers of newsworthiness; coverage in such outlets often triggers broader media attention (Rolling Stone example; Times certifying the 'cocaine issue').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller or regional outlets routinely consult and follow larger papers; trend stories especially gain traction when covered by leading outlets, which function as external benchmarks of quality and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pack coverage versus exclusives as organizational strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations often prefer pack coverage for safety and consistency but seek exclusives ('scoops') as a performance measure and competitive differentiator (examples: Miami Herald Gary Hart expose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusives are exceptional and used to claim special excellence or win awards, but they carry higher risk (being wrong and publicly exposed); routine favoring pack coverage minimizes that risk even at the cost of originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-specific organizational routines (television vs newspapers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different media create different routines: television typically has smaller staffs, greater dependence on PR and routine events, uses reporter 'standups' (which favor snappy language and may omit attribution), relies more on news conferences; newspapers rely more on personal expert sources and background reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcast reporters may have fewer beats, less editorial layers, more immediate editorial decision power, and their video packages are harder to change once filed. These structural differences shape source reliance, story form, and the kinds of distortions that appear in coverage.
